Taylor says Indian High Commissioner didn't raise concerns about policy
Angus Taylor says the Indian High Commissioner did not raise concerns about the Coalition's migration policy.
The opposition leader has also said he's also spoken to the Nepali foreign minister today.
"I do it on a regular basis keeping them up to speed on our policies and talking through how our countries, how great countries can work together," Taylor says."I laid out what our policies were."
"I do it on a regular basis keeping them up to speed on our policies and talking through how our countries, how great countries can work together," Taylor says.
"I laid out what our policies were."
Liberal leader responds to aged care sector's concerns about migration policy
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says international students will still be able to work in aged care despite concerns from the sector about how the Coalition's policy will impact them.
The Coalition will provide people on temporary graduate visas working in critical sectors a pathway to a skilled working visa under its policy.
The Ageing Australia chief executive told ABC Radio National Breakfast he wasn't sure how the Coalition's policy will impact people on visas working as cleaners or cooks in the aged care sector.
The opposition leader says international students will still be able to work in aged care.

"There will still be a very significant number of international students coming to this country, and they will be eligible, to do a certain amount of work, including in that sector. And we know that's important to the sector," Taylor says.
Taylor speaks with Indian High Commissioner about migration policy
On Tuesday, the Coalition released it's policy to bring net overseas migration down to 100,000 for the first two years of government.
Under the opposition's policy, it would increase to 130,000 in the third and 160,000 in the fourth year.
The Coalition will cut graduate, refugee and bridging visas to meet the number.
The opposition leader has been asked about analysis pointing to the fact it might be difficult for the Coalition to reach that number.
But Angus Taylor has sidestepped the question and says the Coalition doesn't want a labour market that is "dependent on guest workers".
But asked if that could disincentivize international students, Taylor says he's spoken with the Indian High Commissioner about the policy.
"Our universities right now should be selling educational excellence. That's what they should be selling, sadly some of them are selling visa pathways and migration pathways," Taylor says.

"We strongly welcome Indian students coming here, building skills, getting ahead and if they have their skills we need to continue on as doctors or engineers or whatever it might be, because we need those skills in this country, then great."
Taylor says PM should step in if NSW doesn't change legislation on planning
Angus Taylor says Anthony Albanese should step in if the NSW government doesn't repeal legislation that led to a landmark High Court decision.
The court found planning authorities are required to consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects.
It was in relation to the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine expansion last year in the New South Wales Court of Appeal.

"This is legislation that has been put in place by the [Chris] Minns government. They should repeal it. And if they don't repeal it, if they don't repeal it, Anthony Albanese should put in place overriding legislation to repeal it," Taylor says.

"It's completely unacceptable that a coal mine, expansion or a coal mine development not proceed because of legislation where there's a requirement to take into consideration the customer's emissions."
Taylor accuses Labor of being 'all over the shop' on ATO credit card payments
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has stepped up for a press conference at Naremburn in Sydney's lower north shore.
Taylor accused the federal government of being "all over the shop" on the Australian Taxation Office's (ATO) ban on using credit cards to pay tax.
This morning, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil told Channel Nine Labor has "real concerns" with the ATO's decision to ban credit card payments, following the Reserve Bank's decision to scrap surcharges.
But Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton told ABC Radio National Breakfast that the government backed the ATO's decision to end credit card payments.

"We've had the housing minister in one place, a small business minister somewhere else, and the de facto treasurer has been saying he's been defending the ATO," Taylor says."In the last couple of days, they've said to small businesses you've got to absorb the surcharges. The hypocrisy of this government knows no bounds because they don't understand enterprise."
"We've had the housing minister in one place, a small business minister somewhere else, and the de facto treasurer has been saying he's been defending the ATO," Taylor says.
"In the last couple of days, they've said to small businesses you've got to absorb the surcharges. The hypocrisy of this government knows no bounds because they don't understand enterprise."
Canavan calls for state, federal parliaments to overturn High Court mine decision
Matt Canavan has weighed in on the High Court's landmark decision about the expansion of the Mount Pleasant coal mine in NSW's Hunter.
The High Court ruled that planning authorities must consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects.
The Nationals leader has called on "all governments" to overturn the High Court's decision by passing laws through state or federal parliaments.

"The courts get to make decisions on these issues but it's the parliament that gets to decide with the laws and it is within the power of the New South Wales government, potentially the federal government as well, to give certainty to coal communities, to coal jobs," Canavan says.
Housing institute hits back at One Nation's rental and migration claims
The Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI) has distanced itself from One Nation, after its research was used for the party's latest policy on migration and rents.
On Wednesday, Senator Pauline Hanson's party pledged that, if elected, One Nation would cut 750,000 temporary visas over three years.
This would result in reducing rent inflation by 6.5 per cent and save $2,818 a year for an average rental by the third year of the party's immigration cuts, according to One Nation.
The party said the internal modelling relied on rental figures from the AHURI, to assume a substantial reduction in demand for rented properties as a result of the migration cuts.
The AHURI said in a statement to the ABC that it was not consulted, the research attributed to it was actually ABS 2021 data, and to be cautious about the modelling claims.
"AHURI was not consulted on, or involved in, the modelling One Nation has undertaken, so we are unable to comment on its reliability or validity," its managing director Tom Alves said.

"We would encourage caution when interpreting this ABS data. For example, it should not be assumed that each temporary migrant occupies an entire property, as several people may share a single home."Some temporary migrants may also live in accommodation owned or provided by their employer or education provider, which may not be available or practical for the general rental market."
"We would encourage caution when interpreting this ABS data. For example, it should not be assumed that each temporary migrant occupies an entire property, as several people may share a single home.
"Some temporary migrants may also live in accommodation owned or provided by their employer or education provider, which may not be available or practical for the general rental market."
Coalition claims Greens are 'outsourcing' defence policy to Russia is 'bollocks', says Shoebridge
Greens leader David Shoebridge has hit back at criticism of his party's policy of not sending military aid to Ukraine, maintaining the Greens support humanitarian and civilian aid to the country.
On the weekend, Shoebridge told The Sydney Morning Herald the Greens opposed Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine but did not support "military aid to Ukraine".
Ukraine's ambassador to Australia Vasyl Myroshnychenko told the ABC he hoped the Greens would "reconsider" its position.
Earlier today on News24, Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson accused the Greens of wanting to "outsource" Australia's defence and foreign policy to Russia.
Shoebridge has called Paterson's comments "complete bollocks" and says the Greens have not changed their position on support for Ukraine.

"We absolutely support Australia giving humanitarian aid, civilian aid to the people of Ukraine, to the Ukrainian government in resisting the illegal invasion from Russia," Shoebridge says."And we have been from day one the strongest proponents for sanctions against Russia."
"We absolutely support Australia giving humanitarian aid, civilian aid to the people of Ukraine, to the Ukrainian government in resisting the illegal invasion from Russia," Shoebridge says.
"And we have been from day one the strongest proponents for sanctions against Russia."
Resources minister plays down High Court ruling on coalmine expansion
Resources Minister Madeleine King has also played down the impact of a landmark High Court decision on the expansion of a NSW mine.
Yesterday, the High Court ruled planning authorities are required to consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects.
The decision was in relation to the expansion of the Mount Pleasant coalmine in the NSW Hunter Valley region.
But King has told ABC's AM program the ruling relates to a "particular" application under a particular law in NSW.
"The High Court ruling is a pretty technical ruling about what a planning commission has to consider when it goes through a planning approvals process," King says.

"The main thing is that people should be reassured that there are no jobs at risk because of this ruling. The Mount Pleasant mine will continue. It will continue under its current operations in 2032."
Duniam says aged care workers are classified as skilled workers under Coalition policy
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam says aged care workers on visas were always carved out of the Coalition's migration policy.
On Tuesday, the Coalition announced plans to slash net overseas migration (NOM) to 100,000 for the first two years, followed by 130,000 in the third and 160,000 in the fourth year.
It will do that with deep cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas.
The opposition says temporary visa holders in the aged care sector will be able to transition to skilled visas, meaning they'll stay in the system.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Duniam says aged care workers have been on the Coalition's skilled workers list.

"The provision for aged care workers to be, as required by the industry, be included in the skills list has been part of the policy all along. And provision for the skills needs we have as a country is at the heart of our policy," Duniam says."We're not going to pick and choose randomly and add things in and take them out just at a whim because someone picks up the phone."

"The provision for aged care workers to be, as required by the industry, be included in the skills list has been part of the policy all along. And provision for the skills needs we have as a country is at the heart of our policy," Duniam says.
"We're not going to pick and choose randomly and add things in and take them out just at a whim because someone picks up the phone."
Assistant minister says cost for goods shouldn't go up due to surcharge ban
Andrew Charlton says he doesn't see why businesses would have to increase prices given credit card process fees have fallen.
The Reserve Bank decided to scrap credit card surcharges from October 1, which cost consumers $1.6 billion a year.
But some businesses say they will have to either absorb the cost of that surcharge or pass the cost onto consumers.
The assistant minister has told ABC Radio National Breakfast the government has reduced processing fees to 0.3 per cent.

"That reduction means that card payments are cheaper for businesses to process. So there's no reason as a result of this reform that consumers should be paying more when they tap their card for a coffee," Charlton says."The cost to the business has gone down, there's no reason why that should be greater than what they were paying before in terms of the price and the surcharge."

"That reduction means that card payments are cheaper for businesses to process. So there's no reason as a result of this reform that consumers should be paying more when they tap their card for a coffee," Charlton says.
"The cost to the business has gone down, there's no reason why that should be greater than what they were paying before in terms of the price and the surcharge."

Charlton says Labor supports ATO's decision to end credit card payments
Digital Economy Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton says the government supports the Australian Tax Office's (ATO) decision to ban credit card tax payments.
The ATO held a snap meeting with angry business groups yesterday that were angered by the department's move. But it didn't back down from its decision to stop accepting credit card payments.
Yesterday, Small Business Minister Anne Aly told ABC's Afternoon Briefing she expected the tax office to "keep speaking" to small businesses and "find a way forward".
This morning, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil told Channel Nine Labor had "real concerns" about the ATO's decision not to accept credit card payments.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Charlton says the ATO can be flexible about tax payments.
"The government supports the ATO's decision. The ATO has made that decision because of the principle of consistency between the private sector and the public sector," Charlton says.

"The reason for this is a reason of consistency between the private sector and the public sector. And that is that if we're saying that surcharges can't exist in the private sector, then surcharges shouldn't exist in the public sector."
ATO gave small business a day's notice of credit card ban
We've heard a bit more from the Australian Tax Office (ATO) following its decision to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1.

Small businesses are angry about the move, saying it's a double standard, but the ATO says it would be untenable to absorb the cost of surcharges and would ultimately result in fewer government services.
A big question for the business community is about who made the decision and when.
The ATO has told the ABC it met with small business groups on September 30 to foreshadow the public announcement the following day, on October 1.
On October 2, the ATO invited business groups to a meeting, held yesterday, "to answer follow-up questions and work through implementation and transitional arrangements for affected taxpayers".
The ATO said it would work with taxpayers to establish alternative payment methods and set up payment plans.

"The ATO will continue to engage with stakeholders, supporting taxpayers and tax practitioners, and seek opportunities to promote awareness through consistent communication and key messages," an ATO spokesperson said.
Business groups and the opposition have called for the ban to be reversed, and now Labor ministers — after last week spruiking the surcharge changes — are also airing some concerns.
Steggall says cost of pre-COP is 'nothing in comparison' to new PNG NRL team
Community Strong MP Zali Steggall says she thinks the Australian-organised pre-COP meeting in Fiji achieved what it set out to do.
Talks are set to wrap up today, with a push to double the number of homes globally, with rooftop solar set to be the main topic of discussion.
But the federal government has come under scrutiny for not attracting world leaders to the event. Just two of the 14 leaders who attended were not from the Pacific.
Steggall has told ABC Radio National Breakfast she thinks the event did amplify Pacific voices.
However, she says Australia should have been represented at the event by a cross-party delegation.
"We have allocated $600 million to establish an NRL team in Papua New Guinea on the national security grounds for geopolitics and relations," Steggall says.

"Now, the cost of this pre-COP is nothing in comparison, and yet will achieve so much more because what it did is it brought together Pacific leaders and nations, ministers, community groups, NGOs to bear witness to what the reality of climate change is for them."
Pre-COP meeting in Fiji to conclude today
The Australian-led climate talks in the Pacific will wrap up today, with a push to double the number of homes globally and rooftop solar the main item on the agenda.
After four days of discussions, pre-COP is drawing to a close and there's been a mixed response to the event.

Pacific communities and leaders have welcomed the opportunity to shine a spotlight on their fight against climate change. They've also attracted funding to better adapt to rising seas and more extreme weather events.
But the Albanese government has been criticised for spending $20 million on the event and failing to attract many world leaders.
Only two of the 14 who turned up hailed from outside of the Pacific.

Today's focus will be the launch of a global plan to double the number of homes with rooftop solar to 300 million by the end of the decade. The Australian government will be asked to sign up to the pledge.
Ayres plays down concerns over landmark High Court ruling
Industry Minister Tim Ayres has played down concerns about a landmark High Court ruling over a NSW coal mine expansion.
The High Court found planning authorities are required to consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects.
The case was brought on by a residents' group opposed to the expansion of the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine in the NSW Hunter region.
The Minerals Council says the decision sends a negative signal to Australia's trade partners.
Speaking on ABC News Breakfast, Ayres says he doesn't think it's a very big deal because he says it is confined to a "particular set of circumstances in New South Wales".
Ayres says it doesn't mean Australia is responsible for scope 3 emissions, which are not accounted for in Australia's emissions.

"It's up to Korea to comply with their obligations or Japan or the United States or all of the South-East Asian economies, for example, which have all got their own emissions obligations that they have signed up to, it's their obligation to do that work," Ayres says.
Labor has 'real concerns' about ATO's decision not to accept credit card payments: O'Neil
Clare O'Neil says the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) should resume discussions with the business sector over its decision not to accept credit card payments for tax bills.
The housing minister says Labor has "real concerns" with the ATO's decision to ban credit card payments, following the Reserve Bank's decision to scrap surcharges.
The ATO met with business groups yesterday angered by the move, but the department did not budge on its decision.
However, O'Neil has defended the Reserve Bank's decision to scrap the fees, which cost consumers $1.6 billion a year.
"We really want the ATO to go back and talk to business about what they've decided to do here, and think about how they can find a solution that works," O'Neil has told Channel Nine.

"You should not be charged to use your own money, and businesses need to be transparent about how much they're charging for products and services. So this is a really good change the government has made."
Nationals frontbencher Bridget McKenzie says ending the surcharge won't make everyday items cheaper.
She says the government needs to direct the ATO to accept credit card payments.

"The prime minister promised that removing the surcharge would make coffees go down. Somehow ebenesco, surchargio, disappearo. Guess what? It doesn't disappear. Businesses are being expected to absorb it," McKenzie says.
